power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Can Human Verification Restore Felt Responsibility for AI-Assisted Knowledge Work?

author.affiliation:
Cologne Institute for Information Systems
								University of Cologne
								
									Germany

Cologne Institute for Information Systems
								University of Cologne
								
									Germany

text.text: Generative AI (genAI) co-produces the work of hundreds of millions of people.
Human oversight, the default safeguard in AI governance, assumes that people still feel responsible for the outputs they approve.
Yet genAI assistance can lower psychological ownership of such outputs, and whether the resulting loss of felt responsibility can be repaired remains unclear.

Drawing on the triangle model of responsibility and psychological ownership theory, we propose that psychological ownership is how people experience the causal link between themselves and an outcome, that genAI assistance weakens this link, and that a mandatory verification step after generation can rebuild it.
We derive five hypotheses on the erosion and restoration of psychological ownership and felt responsibility and on revision after criticism, and we outline a 3 × 2 experiment to test them.
Generative AI (genAI) co-produces the work of hundreds of millions of people.
ChatGPT alone surpassed 800 million weekly active users in 2025 1 , and most organisations and students use such tools routinely 2, 3 .
text.formatted: ChatGPT alone surpassed 800 million weekly active users in 2025 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> , and most organisations and students use such tools routinely <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: As genAI becomes part of everyday infrastructure in law, management, education, and private life, one question gains weight.
When people delegate cognitive work to a machine, do they still hold themselves responsible for the result?
We argue that felt responsibility depends on whether people experience an output as their own.
If genAI assistance weakens this experience, it may also weaken the link between people and the outcomes for which they are formally accountable.
Figure 1 summarises the problem, the study design, and the predicted pattern of results.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> summarises the problem, the study design, and the predicted pattern of results.

text.text: Human oversight is the standard remedy for AI-related error, with a person kept in the loop to check the machine 4, 5 .
text.formatted: Human oversight is the standard remedy for AI-related error, with a person kept in the loop to check the machine <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">5</ref> .

text.text: This remedy assumes that the overseer still feels responsible for what they approve.
In practice, human oversight often falls short 6, 7 .
text.formatted: In practice, human oversight often falls short <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">7</ref> .

text.text: A meta-analysis of 106 experiments found that human-AI combinations frequently perform worse than the better of human or AI alone 8 , and operators often fail to detect errors in reliable automated systems 9 .
text.formatted: A meta-analysis of 106 experiments found that human-AI combinations frequently perform worse than the better of human or AI alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">8</ref> , and operators often fail to detect errors in reliable automated systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9</ref> .

text.text: If genAI further erodes the responsibility people feel, oversight may fail more often.
Whether a concrete oversight step can counter this erosion is therefore a practical question for AI governance.
Philosophers have long argued that AI creates responsibility gaps, in which no human can legitimately be held accountable for machine-mediated outcomes 5, 10 .
text.formatted: Philosophers have long argued that AI creates responsibility gaps, in which no human can legitimately be held accountable for machine-mediated outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">10</ref> .

text.text: These analyses are largely Fig. 1: Study overview.
text.formatted: These analyses are largely Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>: Study overview.

text.text: Left, generative AI increasingly co-produces everyday work, and a pilot study (N = 138) showed that genAI assistance lowers psychological ownership and, through it, felt responsibility.

Middle, the 3 × 2 between-subjects experiment crosses production condition (manual, unverified genAI, genAI with verification) with supervisor feedback (neutral, negative), with 800 participants per cell.
Right, predicted pattern of results.

Unverified genAI assistance is predicted to lower felt responsibility relative to manual production (H1) through reduced psychological ownership (H2), and verification is predicted to partially restore psychological ownership and felt responsibility (H3).

Negative feedback is predicted to increase the probability of revising less after unverified genAI assistance than after manual production (H4) and more after genAI assistance with verification than after unverified genAI assistance (H5).
Bar heights and slopes are schematic and do not represent assumed effect sizes. normative.
They describe what responsibility should look like, not what people actually feel.
Empirical cases point to behavioural consequences.

When a New York court sanctioned lawyers who had filed a brief citing six cases that ChatGPT had invented, the failure lay not with the model alone but with lawyers who had not checked work submitted under their names 11, 12 .
text.formatted: When a New York court sanctioned lawyers who had filed a brief citing six cases that ChatGPT had invented, the failure lay not with the model alone but with lawyers who had not checked work submitted under their names 11, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Delegating to AI can also increase dishonesty 13 , and greater reliance on genAI is associated with less critical engagement with one's own work 14 .
text.formatted: Delegating to AI can also increase dishonesty <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> , and greater reliance on genAI is associated with less critical engagement with one's own work <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: These findings suggest that delegation can change behaviour, but they do not show whether, or why, it changes the responsibility people feel.
Felt responsibility is the psychological state that motivates people to invest effort, scrutinise their output, and uphold standards 15, 16 .
text.formatted: Felt responsibility is the psychological state that motivates people to invest effort, scrutinise their output, and uphold standards <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: According to the triangle model of responsibility, it forms when people perceive a causal connection between their own actions and an outcome, a bond that the model describes as a psychological adhesive (Fig. 2) 15 .
text.formatted: According to the triangle model of responsibility, it forms when people perceive a causal connection between their own actions and an outcome, a bond that the model describes as a psychological adhesive (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: We propose that psychological ownership, the sense that something is mine even without any legal claim 17 , is how people experience this causal connection.
text.formatted: We propose that psychological ownership, the sense that something is mine even without any legal claim <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , is how people experience this causal connection.

text.text: Psychological ownership develops through three routes.
People exercise control over a target, invest the self into it, and come to know it intimately 17, 18 .
text.formatted: People exercise control over a target, invest the self into it, and come to know it intimately <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> .

text.text: Producing something oneself engages all three routes, which is why production fosters psychological ownership, and psychological ownership in turn gives rise to felt responsibility 18, 19 .
text.formatted: Producing something oneself engages all three routes, which is why production fosters psychological ownership, and psychological ownership in turn gives rise to felt responsibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Because we treat felt responsibility as a consequence of psychological ownership rather than as a component of it, we model psychological ownership as the mechanism that links genAI use to felt responsibility.
If psychological ownership is the mechanism, the next question is whether genAI assistance undermines it.

When users delegate generation and interact through prompts, they cede control over how the output takes shape, invest less of themselves than writing would require, and cannot fully know why the output took its form [20] [21] [22] .
text.formatted: When users delegate generation and interact through prompts, they cede control over how the output takes shape, invest less of themselves than writing would require, and cannot fully know why the output took its form <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> .

text.text: Several studies report that genAI use lowers psychological ownership across a range of tasks 20, 22, 23 .
text.formatted: Several studies report that genAI use lowers psychological ownership across a range of tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Whether this loss extends to felt responsibility, and whether it can be reversed, remains unclear.
Because the loss of psychological ownership is already documented, we treat it as a precondition that our paradigm must reproduce before repair can be tested, not as the contribution of this study.

We therefore predict, as a builtin replication, that genAI assistance without a verification step will reduce felt responsibility relative to manual production (H1) and that reduced psychological ownership will mediate this effect (H2, Table 1).
text.formatted: We therefore predict, as a builtin replication, that genAI assistance without a verification step will reduce felt responsibility relative to manual production (H1) and that reduced psychological ownership will mediate this effect (H2, Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: If genAI weakens the causal link between user and output, interventions that rebuild this link should restore felt responsibility.
Interventions that engage users before or during generation can restore psychological ownership 20, 22 .
text.formatted: Interventions that engage users before or during generation can restore psychological ownership <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: Another option is to intervene after generation, by prompting users to review the output against the available information and allowing them to edit it before they submit.
Most genAI tools already allow editing, so such a step should work less by granting control than by prompting people to use it.
It should re-engage control, self-investment, and object knowledge at once.
On this view, oversight becomes a second act of authorship rather than a formality.
We predict that, compared with unverified genAI assistance, a mandatory verification step will partially restore psychological ownership and, through it, felt responsibility (H3, Table 1).
text.formatted: We predict that, compared with unverified genAI assistance, a mandatory verification step will partially restore psychological ownership and, through it, felt responsibility (H3, Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: This prediction bears directly on human-in-the-loop requirements in AI governance, which presume that the person who checks a machine's output still treats that output as their own.
H1 to H3 concern self-reported states, but felt responsibility matters because it shapes behaviour.
People who feel responsible for a piece of work and then receive criticism should feel pressure to revise it, because they experience its shortcomings as their own 24 .
text.formatted: People who feel responsible for a piece of work and then receive criticism should feel pressure to revise it, because they experience its shortcomings as their own <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: When felt responsibility is low, this pressure should be weaker, and flaws in the output may seem to be someone else's problem.
Psychological ownership does not always favour change, however.
People who feel ownership of an idea resist suggestions that remove parts of it but readily adopt suggestions that add to it 25 .
text.formatted: People who feel ownership of an idea resist suggestions that remove parts of it but readily adopt suggestions that add to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: The feedback in this study asks for additions rather than cuts, so psychological ownership should increase rather than reduce revision.

We predict that identical negative feedback will produce a smaller increase in revision after unverified genAI assistance than after manual production (H4) and a larger increase after genAI assistance with verification than after unverified genAI assistance (H5, Table 1).
text.formatted: We predict that identical negative feedback will produce a smaller increase in revision after unverified genAI assistance than after manual production (H4) and a larger increase after genAI assistance with verification than after unverified genAI assistance (H5, Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Revision after criticism thus serves as a behavioural indicator of psychological ownership and shows whether erosion and repair extend from what people report to what they do.
Here we will test H1 to H5 in a 3 × 2 between-subjects experiment.

Participants will complete a knowledge-work task manually, with genAI assistance, or with genAI assistance followed by a mandatory verification step, and will then receive neutral or negative feedback before they can revise.
H1 and H2 reproduce the established erosion as a built-in replication and precondition, whereas H3 and H5 test restoration and form the focus of the study.
Each confirmatory test is paired with an equivalence test, so that null results are informative.
A pilot study supported the core mediation and the feasibility of the paradigm 26 .
text.formatted: A pilot study supported the core mediation and the feasibility of the paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: Table 1 summarises the research questions and hypotheses, and Fig. 3 depicts the hypothesised models.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> summarises the research questions and hypotheses, and Fig. <ref type="figure">3</ref> depicts the hypothesised models.

text.text: Fig. 3: Hypothesised effects. (a) Erosion and restoration of the psychological ownership mechanism.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure">3</ref>: Hypothesised effects. (a) Erosion and restoration of the psychological ownership mechanism.

text.text: Relative to manual production, unverified genAI assistance is predicted to reduce felt responsibility (H1, total effect), mediated by reduced psychological ownership (H2).
Relative to unverified genAI assistance, a mandatory verification step is predicted to restore psychological ownership and, through it, felt responsibility (H3, restoration contrast and mediation).
The direct effect of production condition on felt responsibility is estimated but not hypothesised. (b) Behavioural consequences.
Negative feedback is expected to increase the probability of revising, and production condition is expected to moderate the size of this increase.
H4 compares manual production with unverified genAI assistance, and H5 compares unverified genAI assistance with genAI assistance plus verification.
Both are tested as production by feedback interactions on revision choice across both feedback arms of the 3 × 2 design.
Dashed arrows indicate indirect paths.
Table 1: Research questions and hypotheses.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref>: Research questions and hypotheses.

text.text: H1 and H2 reproduce the erosion of psychological ownership and felt responsibility as a built-in replication.
H3 to H5 test restoration and its behavioural consequences.
The authors declare no competing interests.
S.R. conceived the study, designed the experiment, conducted the pilot study, and wrote the manuscript.
M.W. supervised the project and reviewed and edited the manuscript.
Does unverified genAI assistance reduce felt responsibility?
Felt responsibility will be lower after unverified genAI assistance than after manual production.
Is the erosion mediated by psychological ownership?
The reduction in felt responsibility under unverified genAI assistance will be mediated by reduced psychological ownership, operating through perceived control, self-investment, and object knowledge.
Does verification restore psychological ownership and felt responsibility?

Psychological ownership and felt responsibility will be higher after genAI assistance with verification than after unverified genAI assistance, and the increase in felt responsibility will be mediated by increased psychological ownership.
Does unverified genAI assistance weaken responsiveness to negative feedback?
The increase in the probability of revising under negative relative to neutral feedback will be smaller after unverified genAI assistance than after manual production.
Does verification restore responsiveness to negative feedback?
The increase in the probability of revising under negative relative to neutral feedback will be larger after genAI assistance with verification than after unverified genAI assistance.
A pilot study (N = 138) 26 supported the core mediation from genAI use through reduced psychological ownership to felt responsibility and confirmed the feasibility of the paradigm.
text.formatted: A pilot study (N = 138) <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> supported the core mediation from genAI use through reduced psychological ownership to felt responsibility and confirmed the feasibility of the paradigm.

text.text: GenAI assistance reduced felt responsibility relative to manual production (d = 1.73, 95% CI [1.33, 2.12]), and this effect was fully mediated by reduced psychological ownership (indirect effect b = -1.14, 95% CI [-1.71, -0.68]).

We will test H1 to H5 in a 3 (production condition: manual, unverified genAI, genAI with verification) by 2 (feedback: neutral, negative) between-subjects experiment with 4,800 adults recruited online.
Participants will complete a knowledge-work task.
In the unverified genAI condition, participants can edit the generated text but are not prompted to do so.
In the verification condition, a mandatory step after generation will prompt them to review the output before they submit it.
All participants will then receive neutral or critical feedback and can decide whether to revise.
Each directional test will be paired with an equivalence test, so that null results are informative.
The study has been approved by the Ethical Review Board of the Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, University of Cologne.
Fig 2: The triangle model of responsibility applied to genAI-assisted production.
The figure adapts the triangle model of Schlenker et al. 15 to the three production conditions. (a) In the manual condition, all three links are intact.

The person perceives a causal connection to the outcome (identity-event link), recognises applicable quality standards (prescription-event link), and feels bound by role obligations (prescription-identity link). (b) In the unverified genAI condition, the person delegates composition to the AI, which is expected to weaken the identityevent link.

Felt responsibility should decline (H1), mediated by reduced psychological ownership (H2). (c) In the genAI with verification condition, a mandatory review step after generation prompts the person to check the output and allows them to edit it.

This step is expected to re-engage the control, self-investment, and object knowledge routes to psychological ownership, to partially restore the identity-event link, and thereby to partially restore felt responsibility (H3).
